system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex surgical history, including sclerosing mesenteritis and prior gastrocutaneous fistula, was admitted five days after surgical closure due to increasing pain, erythema, and induration at the incision site. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Imaging revealed a superficial fluid collection, and bedside incision and drainage were performed. Cultures grew Escherichia coli and Proteus vulgaris, both sensitive to antibiotics. She was initially treated with vancomycin for MRSA prophylaxis, but antibiotics were discontinued due to clinical improvement and superficial healing by secondary intention. Pain was managed with IV Dilaudid, then transitioned to acetaminophen. She was discharged home with wound care instructions, a visiting nurse, and follow-up planned. No further antibiotics were prescribed.

previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex surgical history, including sclerosing mesenteritis and prior gastrocutaneous fistula, was admitted five days after surgical closure due to increasing pain, erythema, and induration at the incision site. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Imaging revealed a superficial fluid collection, and bedside incision and drainage were performed. Cultures grew Escherichia coli and Proteus vulgaris, both sensitive to antibiotics. She was initially treated with vancomycin for MRSA prophylaxis, but antibiotics were discontinued due to clinical improvement and superficial healing by secondary intention. Pain was managed with IV Dilaudid, then transitioned to acetaminophen. She was discharged home with wound care instructions, a visiting nurse, and follow-up planned. No further antibiotics were prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re in the ICU right now because you were confused when you came in. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I don’t really remember much. My husband said I was acting strange for two days. I missed my magnesium and potassium pills. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We’re also seeing signs of infection and your liver tests are off. Your ammonia level was high, which can cause confusion. We started you on lactulose and antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so sick lately. I had an endoscopy recently for vomiting, but they didn’t find anything. I didn’t have fever or pain then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Right now, your body is under stress—low potassium, infection, and fluid loss from your stomach tube. We’re giving you fluids and watching your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube is awful. It drained so much. Why did I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bowel wasn’t moving—called ileus. The tube helps relieve pressure and lets your gut rest. We’ll remove it once things improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray shows your colon is still dilated, but no blockage. We’re keeping you on bowel rest for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever eat again? I’m so tired and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you anti-nausea meds. Once your bowel starts moving, we’ll try small sips. It may take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg ultrasound was clear—no clots. But your neck and arm veins show narrowing from past lines. That makes access hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many lines. They always say my veins are bad. Is that why I got sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The femoral line placed at the other hospital may have introduced bacteria. We’re treating it as sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are back. You have three bacteria: Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and Staph. We’ve narrowed your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three? Is that bad? Where did they come from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but treatable. Likely from the femoral line. We’ve removed it and are now on targeted antibiotics—vancomycin and ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my confusion? Is it from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s multifactorial—dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and possibly the infection. Your ammonia is down, and you’re more alert. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT neck shows chronic vein changes from past lines. No acute clot, but explains your swelling. We’ll avoid femoral access in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m swollen everywhere. Is that from the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave a lot of IV fluids to treat sepsis. You’ve gained weight, but it’s temporary. We’ll monitor your legs and you can track your weight at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-ray shows your colon is still dilated, but stable. We’re starting loperamide for diarrhea that started after the ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought the ileus was getting better. Why diarrhea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes after a bowel slowdown, it rebounds. Your C. diff test was negative, so we think it’s from gut imbalance. Loperamide should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was very high—up to 4. We gave vitamin K. It’s improving. Hepatology thinks it’s from poor nutrition, not liver failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take rivaroxaban for clots. Is that why my blood didn’t clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, but your liver wasn’t making clotting factors well. Vitamin K helped, and we’ve continued your rivaroxaban safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need a new IV line. Your femoral line is out, and your upper veins are narrowed. We’re planning a midline in your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please be careful. I’ve had so many failed lines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your midline was placed successfully in your right arm. It’s working well for antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some atelectasis—lung collapse from shallow breathing. We’ll have you use the incentive spirometer often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been too weak to breathe deeply. Will it get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as you feel stronger. It’s not pneumonia, so no extra antibiotics. Just keep using the device and coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving—INR normal, liver tests better, and white count stable. Your bowel is moving again. We’ll start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll advance slowly. If you tolerate it, you can move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Your last X-ray shows big improvement in your colon. We’ll remove the NG tube today if you’re still tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please take it out. I hate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We will. Also, your antibiotics are switching to oral—linezolid and cipro—for one more week at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have to take those? Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to finish treating the infection. Linezolid can affect other meds—don’t take your migraine injections until it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are nearly normal. Potassium is stable, bicarbonate at 21. We’ll stop the oral bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my confusion? Could low blood sugar be causing it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t see low sugar here, but we’ll give you a glucometer to check at home, just in case. Your mental status has cleared, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s from the fluids we gave. We didn’t start a diuretic, but keep weighing yourself. Call if you don’t lose weight in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final X-ray shows your bowel is much better. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if you keep doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish your antibiotics, take your potassium twice daily now, monitor your weight, and check your blood sugar if you feel off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them—rivaroxaban, gabapentin, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, PPI, and the rest. We’re sending a list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor and primary care. Labs next week to check electrolytes and blood count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your midline will be removed before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: finish antibiotics, monitor weight and blood sugar, and call if you’re not improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no femoral lines ever again, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ll note your difficult access. Use your arm veins when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming: you understand your meds, warning signs, and follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—antibiotics for four more days, potassium twice daily, weigh daily, check sugar if confused, and see my doctors next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Midline is out, no bleeding. You’re ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you to check in. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let the nurse know when you’re ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history including sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic bowel obstruction, and line-associated DVTs was transferred to this hospital with altered mental status, bacteremia, and ileus. She had been confused for two days, attributed initially to missed magnesium and potassium supplements. Workup revealed polymicrobial bacteremia (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus epidermidis) from a femoral central line, acute toxic encephalopathy likely due to dehydration and metabolic stress, colonic ileus requiring NG tube decompression, and coagulopathy responsive to vitamin K. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics, later transitioned to oral linezolid and ciprofloxacin, bowel rest, and supportive care. Her mental status, bowel function, and labs improved. A midline catheter was placed for ongoing access. She developed iatrogenic peripheral edema from fluid resuscitation, managed conservatively. She was discharged home with oral antibiotics, increased potassium supplementation, a glucometer for monitoring, and plans for outpatient follow-up.
